observation: Dual coding theory (Paivio) holds that verbal and nonverbal (imagery) information are processed by partially independent but interconnected cognitive subsystems; concrete/imageable material can be stored both verbally and visually, giving a retrieval advantage over verbal-only material.
claim: Pairing a compact apt visual with concise text can beat either alone for concrete/imageable content, but only if the two channels aren't simply re-saying the same content in the same modality at the same time.
mechanism: Dual-coded information has two independent retrieval routes (verbal and imagistic), increasing the odds of successful recall versus single-coded verbal-only information.
context: foundational cognitive psychology, replicated across many studies

implications.text: When content-type-aware formatting adds a diagram/visual alongside text, ensure the visual adds genuinely new (non-redundant) information rather than restating the text.

observation: Picture superiority is large and replicated in recognition/recall (d~1.5-2.0 in some meta-analytic estimates), but a meta-analysis of the 'multimedia effect in problem solving' found no significant effect on response time when pictures were added to problem text, and the effect is driven by concrete/imageable content.
claim: Riemann's primary content (email, notes, docs) is mostly abstract/verbal, so a generic decorative icon next to abstract paragraphs should not be expected to deliver a memory or speed boost; only a genuinely apt diagram of concrete content (e.g. a real flowchart of a real process) would.
mechanism: Picture superiority depends on the content being concrete/imageable enough to be dual-coded; abstract verbal content has little or nothing to visually encode.
context: lab, memory/recognition tasks and a problem-solving meta-analysis

implications.text: Do not add decorative icons to abstract L0-L2 content expecting a comprehension/memory win; reserve auto-generated visuals for content that is genuinely concrete/structural (comparisons, timelines, processes).

observation: Mayer & Moreno's modality effect (53/61 supporting tests, median d=0.76) shows narration+diagram beats on-screen text+diagram for short/simple content, but this reverses for long/complex/self-paced material (Leahy & Sweller's transient-information effect, replicated in a 2022 VR study): text+diagram beats narration+diagram because speech is transient (can't be re-read) and overloads working memory, while text supports self-pacing and rereading.
claim: Audio's advantage over text is real only for short/simple material or when pacing is user-controlled; for long/complex content, text (or user-pausable audio) wins because it supports rereading and self-pacing.
mechanism: Spoken narration is transient and cannot be reread, so for long/complex content it overloads working memory in a way self-paced rereadable text does not.
population: general learners (multimedia learning studies, replicated at least twice including one VR study)

implications.text: Make TTS-on-L0/L1 (short content) a one-tap default; require an explicit user choice to start TTS on the full L3, always with a visible scrub/pause control.

observation: The redundancy effect (well-replicated Mayer principle) shows presenting identical information simultaneously in two channels (e.g. on-screen text exactly duplicating narration) hurts learning relative to narration alone or text alone, because reconciling the two channels wastes working memory.
claim: If Riemann adds a 'read aloud' feature, it should not simultaneously display and word-for-word highlight identical text at reading pace as the default; a light 'currently reading paragraph N' indicator is preferable to literal karaoke-style redundant captioning.
mechanism: Reconciling two channels carrying identical content imposes an extraneous processing cost of cross-checking rather than adding independent information.

implications.text: Avoid literal word-for-word synchronized captioning as the default TTS UI; use a lighter paragraph-level 'currently reading' indicator instead.

observation: Pashler et al. 2008 (commissioned by APS) found essentially no crossover-interaction evidence supporting the 'learning styles' matching hypothesis (matching instruction modality to a learner's self-reported preferred style); only one study had the necessary design and it didn't clearly support meshing.
claim: Riemann should never ask 'are you a visual or audio person' as a setup question or infer and lock in a fixed per-user modality preference; content-structure fit (not person-trait fit) is the real, distinct, well-supported claim.
population: general learners (commissioned review of the learning-styles literature)
context: commissioned literature review finding essentially no supporting crossover-interaction evidence

implications.text: Never build a fixed 'preferred modality' user profile or onboarding question; let modality choice be state-dependent (what was picked last time, under what load) and content-dependent, never a locked-in trait.

observation: Clinton-Lisell 2022 meta-analysis (k=46 studies, n=4,687, fact-checked confirmed) found no reliable average difference between listening and reading comprehension (g=0.07, n.s.); reading wins when self-paced (g=0.13) and when the test measures inferential rather than literal comprehension (g=0.36 for inferential); listening was not reliably better in any subgroup.
claim: Audio is not an inherent downgrade from text for gist-level content generally, but for anything requiring inference (the kind of synthesis an L0/L1 gist should support) or anything the user will want to re-scan, text or user-pausable audio has a real edge; audio's disadvantage is about pacing control, not the ear being an inferior channel.
mechanism: Reading allows self-paced control (rereading, skimming ahead) that listening does not unless the audio interface supports scrubbing/rewind equally well.
population: general readers/listeners (mixed ages, mostly neurotypical or unspecified, structured study conditions)

implications.text: Build a good scrubbing/rewind/pause UI on the audio channel to close most of the reading-vs-listening gap, especially since Riemann's L0/L1 gists require inferential understanding.

observation: Murphy et al. 2022 (fact-checked, minor correction: no reliable cost up to 2x, cost specifically emerges at 2.5x) found lecture-video playback speed up to ~2x causes essentially no measurable loss in immediate or delayed comprehension versus 1x; costs appear past ~2.5x. A companion body of research flags a metacognitive risk: felt comprehension can decouple from actual comprehension at higher speeds (overconfidence).
claim: A user-controlled playback-speed dial up to ~2x is well justified as a default, free-efficiency control on Riemann's audio output; push past 2x with a soft 'you may be overestimating retention' affordance rather than a hard block.
population: general learners (lecture-video study, not conversational podcasts or dense technical prose)
context: well-designed lab study; generalization to non-lecture audio content is untested

implications.text: Ship a playback-speed control (1x-2x safe default range, soft warning past 2x) as a first-class control on any TTS/audio output.

observation: Nesbit & Adesope 2006 (67 effect sizes, 55 studies, n=5,818, Grade 4-postsecondary) found node-link concept/knowledge maps outperform text/outline conditions on recall and transfer, with larger effects when students construct the map themselves rather than passively view one made for them.
claim: Exposing the abstraction tree as a navigable graph/map, especially with light user-editable interaction (pin/rename/reorder a node), is strongly supported evidence for a v1.x feature, not just a future spatial-view idea -- Riemann's parent/child tree already is a concept map with no LLM-graph-extraction risk since structure comes from the chunker, not from an LLM inferring relationships from prose.
mechanism: Node-link representations make hierarchical/relational structure directly visible, and actively constructing or manipulating the map recruits additional generative/elaborative processing beyond passive reading.
population: students Grade 4 through postsecondary, multiple domains (classroom/study contexts, recall on a later test)
context: large meta-analysis; classroom/study outcome measures, not a live skim-now-maybe-never-test use case

implications.text: Offer a collapsible/zoomable node-link rendering of the L2 section tree alongside the linear markdown view.
Let users lightly interact with the tree (pin, rename, reorder a node) to capture some of the constructing-beats-viewing boost without requiring them to build the tree from scratch.

observation: Convergent (but not single-meta-analysis-unified) instructional-design guidance maps content structure to visual form: causal/process content to flowcharts, hierarchical content to tree/concept maps, comparative content to tables, temporal content to timelines, quantitative content to charts, procedural content to numbered steps/worked examples (Tversky's Congruence Principle).
claim: Content-type-aware auto-formatting (rendering a detected comparison as a table, a detected timeline as a timeline) is a well-motivated but expert-consensus-level (not meta-analytically proven per content type) heuristic worth implementing opportunistically, not as a core v1 requirement.
mechanism: Per the Congruence Principle, the visual form should mirror the structure of the content it represents so the reader doesn't have to mentally re-map an ill-fitting representation.
population: general (composite of instructional-design literature, no single unifying meta-analysis)

implications.text: If the summariser already emits a content-type hint per section, use it to opportunistically pick a rendering primitive (table/timeline/flowchart), but do not require this for v1.

observation: Individual studies find infographics improve comprehension/recall vs text-only (e.g. an orthopaedic journal-club study: ~2/3 correct on infographic-paired papers vs <1/2 text-only), but search results explicitly note inconsistency across the literature and no rigorous meta-analysis isolating infographics from confounds like added effort/novelty was found.
claim: 'Infographic' should be treated as a composite of already-validated primitives (dual coding, concept-map structure, comparison tables) rather than a separate mechanism requiring its own distinct 'infographic mode.'
population: general (mixed studies, one clinical journal-club study)
context: individual studies, inconsistent literature, no unifying meta-analysis

implications.text: Do not build a distinct 'infographic mode'; compose the existing dual-coding, concept-map, and table primitives instead.

observation: 2025-2026 benchmarks (DiagramEval, MermaidSeqBench) exist specifically because LLM text-to-diagram generation accuracy is not yet reliable, scoring across syntax validity, structural accuracy, semantic fidelity and completeness; refining an initial extraction with a second vision-capable LLM pass is one mitigation found.
claim: LLM-generated diagrams/concept maps from arbitrary external prose are not yet trustworthy without structural validation, but an auto-generated node-link view of Riemann's own existing parent/child tree carries no such extraction risk since it needs no LLM-inferred graph structure.
mechanism: A one-shot LLM pass at extracting graph structure from free text is failure-prone; constrained DSLs (e.g. Mermaid syntax) and a second critique/repair pass reduce but don't eliminate hallucinated structure.
population: general (2025-2026 arXiv benchmarks, not yet peer-reviewed-confirmed)

implications.text: If Riemann ever auto-generates diagrams/concept maps of external prose (beyond the tree's own existing structure), validate structurally (schema + edge-reference checks) and consider a second critique/repair LLM pass, mirroring the existing retry-on-validation-failure pattern.

observation: Tversky & Morrison found animation is not inherently superior to static sequences for learning; apparent wins for animation are usually confounded by animation conveying more information (continuous motion, microsteps) rather than modality per se -- animation should be reserved for genuinely continuous/dynamic content (the Congruence Principle).
claim: Riemann's planned animated zoom-dial transition (anchoring/scroll behaviour) is defensible under the Congruence Principle because the information the animation conveys -- 'this passage's position in the abstraction hierarchy is preserved across a zoom' -- is itself inherently continuous/spatial information, not decoration.
context: highly cited, foundational, though from 2002; a 2016 meta-analysis exists but was not read in full

implications.text: Retain animated level-transitions in the zoom dial as evidence-aligned (conveying genuinely continuous positional information), not merely decorative.

observation: Task-switching literature shows measurable modality-shift costs even for purely response/stimulus modality changes; a late-2025 HCI paper proposes a 'Modality-Switch Cognitive Cost' (MSCC) metric for multimodal interaction design specifically, citing large performance variance explained by modality condition.
claim: Letting a user flip modality (text/audio/diagram) at any abstraction level is desirable for adaptivity, but each switch is not free -- it is more like a level-change-plus-something, so modality choice should be a separate, sticky control from the zoom dial rather than resetting or auto-switching on every level change.
mechanism: Switching between modalities imposes a task-set reconfiguration cost distinct from and additive to any content-processing cost.
population: general (task-switching literature is well-established; MSCC interaction-design framing is a single recent, unreplicated paper)
context: long, replicated cognitive-psychology literature plus one very recent, unverified HCI framing paper

implications.text: Make the zoom dial (level change) and a modality toggle visually/interactionally distinct controls, with modality persisting across dial movements rather than resetting; never auto-switch modality without the user asking, only offer it (e.g. a gentle 'want this read aloud instead?' prompt).

observation: A dedicated meta-analysis (PMC8219577) and Willingham's 'psychologically privileged' framing (found mainly in secondary summaries) show narratively structured content (causal, goal-driven) is recalled and comprehended better than expository content of equivalent informational content.
claim: For content with a natural causal/temporal arc (an email thread, a project timeline, a decision's rationale), Riemann's L0/L1 gist generation should preserve causal/narrative connectives ('X happened, which led to Y') rather than flattening to a bag of facts, as a cheap prompt-engineering win.
mechanism: Causal, goal-structured story form matches a highly familiar cognitive schema and creates a natural retrieval web, unlike a list of disconnected facts.
context: dedicated meta-analysis for the general effect; Willingham's specific 'privileged' framing found only in secondary summaries

implications.text: Prompt L0/L1 summarisation to preserve causal/narrative connectives when the source content has them, rather than compressing to a flat list of facts.

observation: For novices, studying worked examples produces better learning and transfer than solving equivalent problems from scratch (well-replicated CLT effect), because it offloads extraneous problem-solving search, leaving capacity for schema formation; the effect shrinks or reverses with expertise.
claim: When the chunker/summariser encounters a clearly procedural passage (numbered steps, a walked-through calculation, code), it should be preserved close to verbatim at L2 as a protected atomic unit rather than abstracted into a gist, since compressing worked examples destroys the information that makes them pedagogically effective.
mechanism: Worked examples let a novice study a complete correct solution path without the extraneous cognitive cost of generating it themselves via trial and error.
context: one of the best-replicated CLT-derived effects

implications.text: Treat detected worked examples/procedural passages as protected, low-priority-to-summarize atomic units at L2, similar to how code blocks are often protected from summarization.

observation: Narrative-biased summarisation risks inserting a causal interpretation the source didn't actually assert, since pushing causal/narrative framing onto ambiguous content (e.g. someone else's email) can misrepresent it as more causally certain than it is.
claim: Applying the narrative-connectives implication (F04-14) carries a faithfulness/correctness risk, not just a UX one, and should be balanced against grounding/faithfulness requirements.
population: n/a (design-risk observation flagged by the report author)
context: self-identified caveat, not a separate empirical study

implications.text: When prompting for causal/narrative connectives (F04-14), constrain the model to only assert causal links the source text actually supports, and check this against the faithfulness score.
